Last updated November 14, 2026.

Austin housing at a glance

  • Owner-occupied homes: 195,678. Renter-occupied homes: 244,616, so about 44% of occupied homes are owner-occupied.
  • Median gross rent: $1,655 a month.
  • Median year homes were built: 1993.
  • Vacant housing units: 26,134 of 466,428 total.
Selling in Austin?

Get My Cash Offer →

Selling a house in Austin FAQ

How much is a house worth in Austin?

The Census Bureau's 2019-2023 survey puts the median value of owner-occupied homes in Austin at $512,700.

Which sale routes suit an Austin owner who needs to move quickly?

Austin owners generally choose between a standard listing, a self-managed sale and a straight cash purchase. A cash buyer closes on a date you pick and buys the property in whatever state it is in, whereas a listing depends on showings, appraisals and the next buyer's financing.

Prices run high. The Census Bureau's 2020-2024 figures put a typical owned home at $555,300, and only 43.4 percent of households own the home they occupy. With so many renters, plenty of Austin houses have been rentals or could become one, which affects what an investor will pay and how fast the deal can move.

  • Standard listing: fits an updated house priced near its closest comparable sales, with weeks to spare for showings and a buyer's lender.
  • Self-managed sale: you handle pricing, contracts and negotiation, and a title company still runs the closing.
  • Cash purchase: fits deferred maintenance, an inherited house, a tenant who is staying, or a hard deadline.

What shaped Austin's neighborhoods, and why would a buyer care?

The city was platted in 1839 as the capital of the young Republic of Texas, and the housing here reflects layers of growth from that first grid to the chip-making boom. Commissioners bought 7,735 acres along the Colorado River that included the hamlet of Waterloo, then platted a 640-acre grid between Waller Creek on the east and Shoal Creek on the west, split by Congress Avenue.

The city won the statewide vote to stay the capital in 1872, and the University of Texas was chosen as its site in 1881. Dams on the Colorado River in 1940 and 1941 ended the flooding that had ravaged the town and created Lake Austin and Lake Travis. High technology took off after IBM located here in 1967, followed by Texas Instruments in 1969 and Motorola in 1974.

Fast growth set off resistance by the 1970s. Neighborhood groups, more than 150 by 1983, fought apartment complexes and clogged roads, and environmental ordinances protected creeks, lakes and wooded hills. A seller with an addition built without a permit, or a lot beside a creek, should expect questions from a buyer's inspector.

Where does Austin sit on the map, and what do its creeks and lakes mean for a house?

Austin sits where the Hill Country and the Edwards Plateau meet the Colorado River, on Interstate 35 in central Travis County. The original 640-acre town ran from the river up to Capitol Square between Waller Creek and Shoal Creek, and the incorporated area has grown far past that: from about 31 square miles in 1940 to 225.40 square miles by 1990, and a land area of 319.94 square miles in 2020.

Water shaped the place. Tom Miller Dam, finished in 1940, formed Lake Austin, and Mansfield Dam followed in 1941 to hold back Lake Travis. The Handbook of Texas credits the dams with ending the floods that had hit the town as recently as 1935. The city acquired the spring-fed Barton Springs pool in 1918, and a downtown lake was impounded in 1960. Buyers know the waterways, so a house near a creek or on one of the lakes may draw questions about flood exposure that a house on higher ground will not.

Bergstrom Air Force Base, which began as an Army air base in 1942, stayed open until 1993, and a new convention center opened in 1992. State government, the university and technology employers have anchored the local economy since the mid-twentieth century.

How large and how costly is the Austin housing market?

Austin's July 2025 population estimate is 1,002,632, about 4.6 percent higher than the 958,151 baseline for April 2020. The 2010 Census counted 790,390.

About 78.8 percent of residents stayed at the same address over the prior year, and 59.6 percent of adults 25 or older have finished a bachelor's degree or more. The average commute is 23.7 minutes.

How do Austin's short-term rental licenses work for a seller?

A license belongs to its holder and cannot be passed on, so a buyer who wants nightly guests must apply for a fresh one. The city confirms that short-term rental operating licenses are non-transferable.

In February 2025 Council made short-term rental a secondary use on residential property in every zoning district for anyone holding a license. Changes in October 2025 stretched each license to two years and dropped the occupancy certificate and insurance proof for new applicants and renewals. Tenants may now run one with the landlord's permission.

  • One person may run two units on a single-family site, and any more must be 1,000 feet apart.
  • On multifamily sites the cap is the larger of one unit or a tenth of the units.
  • A local contact must be in Travis, Williamson, Hays, Bastrop or Caldwell County and reachable within two hours.
  • Properties within 100 feet receive written notice of that contact at issuance and renewal.
  • Since July 1, 2026, booking platforms must show license numbers and pull unlicensed listings when the city asks.

Land in the extraterritorial jurisdiction needs no city license or local hotel tax, so check the jurisdiction map on the city's short-term rental page before telling a buyer what is allowed.

How do homestead exemptions and the appraisal cap affect an Austin sale?

If you live in the house, your taxable value is probably below the market value a buyer sees on the listing. Texas school districts exempt $140,000 of a homestead, and the appraised value of a homestead cannot rise more than 10 percent a year beyond new improvements.

That cap follows the owner who claimed the exemption, so an investor starts without it. Have the title company work out the buyer's first full-year tax bill so nothing in the contract is a surprise. Owners past 65 or with a disability also receive $60,000 more in school exemption and a school tax ceiling that can transfer to a new Texas homestead.

Travis County's tax office explains that the Travis Central Appraisal District grants exemptions while the tax office collects bills; its tax breaks page links to each one. The Comptroller's limitations page covers the cap and the ceiling.

What steps and paperwork close an Austin sale?

The deed is the closing document. It must be acknowledged before a notary, or sworn before two witnesses, before the county clerk will record it.

  1. Collect your deed, payoff letters and the latest tax statement.
  2. Request a payoff for any lien, since each year's tax lien attaches January 1.
  3. Check which county records the deed for your parcel, because the city is large.
  4. Sign the settlement papers and deed, and let the title company file the deed.

An inherited house adds a title question: an executor's deed, a muniment of title order or an affidavit of heirship. The last is a sworn statement that no law makes a third party accept, so ask early which one the title insurer will honor.

How should I compare offers on an Austin house?

Compare what lands in your account and when, not the headline figure. A higher price loaded with repair credits, a long financing window and a commission can net less than a lower cash bid with a firm date.

Ask each buyer how they treat tenants, unpermitted work and open code complaints, and whether the bid survives an inspection. Note each deadline in writing and choose the offer that clears your payoff and fits your move.

More questions about Austin, TX

Can an Austin short-term rental license be handed to the new owner?

No. The city says operating licenses cannot be transferred, so a buyer must apply for a new one. Give the buyer your license history so the application goes smoothly.

Is Austin in Travis County?

Austin is the Travis County seat, and the city sits in the central part of the county. Check your tax bill for the county of record on your parcel, since it decides which clerk files the deed.

Does my homestead tax cap pass to the person who buys my Austin house?

No. The cap starts the January after an owner first qualifies for the exemption, so a buyer who moves in and applies starts a new one. A buyer who rents the house out cannot claim it.

What if my Austin house has unpaid property taxes?

The balance is paid out of your sale proceeds, because the lien sticks to the property. Unpaid bills turn delinquent on February 1, with a six percent penalty and one percent interest.

What is Austin's population and size?

The Census Bureau estimates 1,002,632 residents for 2025, a 4.6 percent rise over the 2020 base. The land area is 319.94 square miles.

  • Median year homes were built: 1985.

Selling in Arlington?
We buy Arlington houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Selling a house in Arlington FAQ

How much is a house worth in Arlington?

The Census Bureau's 2019-2023 survey puts the median value of owner-occupied homes in Arlington at $276,400.

Who buys a house in Arlington, TX, and how quickly can a sale close?

Arlington sellers deal with three kinds of buyers: households using a mortgage, other individuals paying out of pocket, and investors who purchase houses in whatever shape they are in. Closing speed turns on the buyer: cash moves when the title work is done, while a loan needs an appraisal and underwriting first.

The Census Bureau counts 402,134 people in the city for mid-2025. Just over half of the homes, 54.3 percent, are lived in by the people who own them, so a seller here competes with many rentals and other resale houses.

  • Financed buyer: tends to pay most for an updated house, but an appraisal or inspection can sink the deal.
  • Individual cash buyer: still negotiates repairs and usually wants a typical inspection period.
  • Investor: prices the repairs in, skips showings and agrees to a date that fits your move, a probate schedule or a lender's deadline.

How did a railroad stop between Dallas and Fort Worth turn into this city?

Arlington started as a market town on the Texas and Pacific Railway in 1876 and was incorporated in 1884, according to the Handbook of Texas. A Presbyterian minister who surveyed land beside the new tracks is credited with the first town plat, and the post office was renamed Arlington in 1877.

Farm trade carried the town for decades. Then came the postwar surge: 7,692 residents in 1950, 44,775 in 1960, 160,123 in 1980 and 261,717 in 1990. A General Motors assembly plant began production in January 1954, Lake Arlington was built in the mid-1950s as a water supply, and the turnpike that became Interstate 30 opened in 1957. Six Flags Over Texas arrived in 1961, and the Rangers moved to town in 1971.

The University of Texas at Arlington grew out of a vocational college founded in 1917 and enrolled 41,515 students in September 2021. The school district ran 78 schools that year. AT&T Stadium has been the Cowboys' home since 2009, and the 5,000-acre Great Southwest Industrial District, shared with Grand Prairie, dates from the turnpike era. Houses built in the boom decades sit beside newer subdivisions, so an older home's roof, foundation and wiring are worth a look before a buyer's inspector does it for you.

What do the 2020-2024 Census estimates say about Arlington housing costs?

A typical Arlington owner-occupied home was worth $304,700 in the latest five-year estimates, and a typical renter paid $1,470 a month. Treat both as middle-of-the-road numbers: a house in a tired condition or in a less sought-after pocket will sit below them.

The city holds 4,112.7 residents per square mile. Roughly 86.7 percent of people over age one stayed in the same home through the prior year, which signals a settled base of neighbors and potential buyers.

Does an Arlington short-term rental permit move to the buyer?

No. The city ties each short-term rental permit to one owner and one address, and it cannot be transferred or assigned, so whoever buys your house must apply on their own.

Arlington defines a short-term rental as a home or part of one used for lodging for fewer than 30 consecutive days. Council approved the rules in April 2019, and rentals running before the August 1, 2019 start date were not grandfathered. Houses qualify in a zone anchored on the Entertainment District, in medium-density and multifamily residential districts, and in some commercial and mixed-use districts.

  • Occupancy tops out at two guests per bedroom plus two, up to 12 people.
  • Amplified sound and outdoor gatherings are off limits from 10 p.m. to 9 a.m.
  • Converting space into extra bedrooms is prohibited and can lower the allowed headcount.
  • Three citations in a year, or ignoring a written notice for ten days, can lead to revocation.

If your house has hosted guests, collect the permit, and the inspection checklist results before you show it. The city's short-term rental page lists what inspectors check, including smoke alarms, escape windows, a posted floor plan and a fire extinguisher.

What property tax dates should an Arlington seller watch?

Texas appraises on January 1, so the owner on that date carries the year's liability, and Arlington bills arrive about October 1. Notices of value for homesteads land near April 1. A homeowner who disagrees with the figure has until May 15, or 30 days after the notice, whichever falls later, to file a protest with the appraisal review board.

Payment is due by January 31 for most accounts. Paying in two halves is allowed, with November 30 and June 30 as the marks. Miss the January cutoff and February 1 brings a six percent penalty with one percent interest; by July the penalty grows to 12 percent. Because the lien for the year attaches in January, a house that closes in March still has to settle that year's bill.

  • School districts exempt $140,000 of a homestead's value.
  • Homeowners aged 65 or older, or disabled, gain another $60,000 school exemption and a ceiling on school tax.
  • If you sell after January 1 to someone who will live in the house, that buyer may be able to claim the exemption at once when you had not.

The Comptroller posts the calendar on its deadlines page. For a payoff on your own account, contact the Tarrant County offices that cover your address.

What documents does an Arlington closing require?

Ownership passes when a signed, acknowledged deed goes into the property records of the county where the lot sits. Texas will file a conveyance only after a notary or similar officer has taken the signer's acknowledgment, or two witnesses have sworn to it.

Pull these together before accepting an offer:

  • your current deed and photo ID
  • mortgage and home-equity payoff statements
  • this year's tax statement and any back-tax notices
  • HOA payoff and transfer paperwork, if one applies
  • leases, deposits and tenant contacts, if someone lives there
  • any rental permit and inspection records

A house that came through an estate needs the right title paper. Executors use an executor's deed; a muniment of title order works when a will is probated without administration; and an affidavit of heirship is only a sworn, court-unverified statement that a title company may decline.

How should I weigh a cash offer against listing the house?

Count what each path leaves you after payoffs, repairs and time. A listing can bring a higher price for a well-kept house, but a cash sale removes the repair list, the open houses and the chance that a buyer's loan falls through.

Collect each offer in writing: the price, the closing date, who pays settlement charges and any exit clauses. Ask whether the buyer will take the house with a tenant or with open city notices. Subtract your payoffs and carrying costs, then choose the figure and date that fit your plans.

More questions about Arlington, TX

Will a buyer pay for a house in Arlington that needs a new roof?

Yes, investors and cash buyers regularly take on roof work, and the offer reflects it. Nothing has to be repaired before closing, so compare the offer with a repaired house's likely price after your own repair bills.

Can I sell a house in Arlington that has been used as an Airbnb?

Yes. The permit stays behind, because it belongs to the owner and address, so the buyer files a new application and passes the city's inspection. Say plainly whether the address sits inside an eligible zone.

What happens to unpaid tax when my Arlington sale closes?

Whatever is owed comes out of your proceeds when you sign, since the lien stays on the house. Ask the tax office for a payoff figure early so the closing statement has no surprise.

Where is the deed filed after an Arlington sale?

At the county clerk's office for the county where the house stands, Tarrant County for most Arlington addresses. A lot near a county line is worth confirming against your tax bill.

How large is Arlington by population and area?

The Census Bureau estimates 402,134 residents for 2025 and counted 142,455 households in 2020-2024. The land area is 95.87 square miles.

What is the quickest way to sell a house in Amarillo?

Sell through an agent if the house is in good shape and you can wait for a financed buyer, or sell for cash if speed, repairs or a tenant make a traditional listing hard. Amarillo is the commercial center of the Texas Panhandle, and mid-2025 estimates count 205,130 residents.

Amarillo is large, and it sits in two counties, so the first step is to find out which county your house is in. The city lies mostly in Potter County and extends into Randall County, which means the tax office, the clerk and the appraisal records you deal with depend on the parcel.

  • Look up the address with the Potter Randall Appraisal District, which determines ownership for both counties.
  • Call the tax office named on your tax statement early in the process.
  • Ask the City of Amarillo's Building Safety office about any open permits on the property.

What does Amarillo's housing market look like in Census data?

Amarillo is an affordable Texas city, with a median home value under $200,000 and about four in ten households renting. The Census Bureau's QuickFacts table shows the figures below, and the city's 2020 population count was 200,393, compared with 190,695 in 2010.

Amarillo city, Texas: housing, income and commuting figures from the Census Bureau

A mean commute of 19.6 minutes is short for a city of 102 square miles. The Census Bureau also counts 10,973 veterans in the 2020-2024 estimates, so disabled veteran exemptions are worth asking about when you sell or buy.

How did Amarillo develop, and what does it mean for homes today?

Amarillo was platted in April 1887 along the Fort Worth and Denver City Railway in Potter County and named for a nearby lake and creek, probably after the yellow soil or spring wildflowers. The Texas State Historical Association says the first site was on low ground that would flood, so a rancher and his partner bought land to the east in 1888 and drew merchants to higher ground. By 1890 the town's center had moved a mile east, and the county seat followed in 1893.

The economy grew from cattle shipping into wheat, gas, oil and helium. Gas was discovered in 1918 and oil in 1921, and the Cliffside field's helium led to a federal helium plant in 1928. In World War II Amarillo hosted an Army Air Field and the nearby Pantex plant, and the city's population hit 51,686 by 1940. Interstate 40 and Interstate 27 later pulled new housing and shopping toward the south and west, according to the Handbook of Texas.

The same source describes a city that by 1980 had 149,230 residents and more than sixty square miles within Potter and Randall counties. Gas, petroleum, agriculture and cattle remain the entry's named income sources, and the Census data shows a large health care sector, with healthcare receipts of $2,777,390 thousand in 2022.

How do taxes work for a house in the Randall County part of Amarillo?

Randall County's tax office mails statements each October 1, and they are due on receipt. Paying by January 31 avoids penalty and interest, and February 1 starts delinquency. A payment sent by first-class mail counts as paid on the date of the post office cancellation mark.

The Randall County tax office also explains how a sale affects the bill:

  • The taxing unit does not prorate the year. Most sales contracts split the year's taxes between buyer and seller, so check the contract and closing statement.
  • Whoever owned the house on the first of January of the prior year remains liable for that year's tax, and the unit can also pursue the buyer through the lien.
  • Over-65, disabled and veteran homesteads can pay in four installments, with the first fourth and a signed agreement due by January 31. A first payment received by February 28 carries 7% penalty and interest, and a missed installment adds 6% penalty plus 1% interest each month.

A tax certificate shows delinquent taxes, penalties and interest for each taxing unit. The fee is $10, paid in certified funds at pickup, and you can request it by email and pick it up at either the Canyon or the Amarillo office. If taxes are due and you want a zero-balance certificate, pay with cash or certified funds or wait 10 working days for a check to clear.

The Potter Randall Appraisal District is at 5701 Hollywood Road, Amarillo, with a phone number of 806-358-1601 and a mailing address of P.O. Box 7190, Amarillo, TX 79114. For a parcel in Potter County, ask the Potter County tax assessor-collector for the same certificate.

Which Amarillo permit and platting rules affect a sale?

Amarillo's Building Safety office is in the Simms Municipal Building at 808 S Buchanan Street, Suite 104, open weekdays from eight to five, and permits go through the MGO Connect online portal. The city's ordinance Sec. 4-10-21 says land cannot be used unless a Certificate of Occupancy and Compliance has been issued.

A Certificate of Occupancy is issued automatically for new buildings when the permit is completed. A separate certificate is needed when the use changes or when none was ever issued, and alterations require a remodel or repair permit with a registered contractor. For a house with a converted garage, a rented room or a business use, ask Building Safety whether the certificate matches what the house is today.

Platting matters if you want to sell part of a lot. The county's FAQ explains that a plat is required when land is divided for sale, and that in Amarillo it applies to any tract inside the city limits and to tracts of five acres or less in the extraterritorial jurisdiction extending five miles beyond the limits.

Does flood risk affect an Amarillo sale?

It can. The original town site was moved to higher ground after flooding concerns in 1888 and 1889, and drainage on the High Plains is still a buyer question. Randall County's floodplain page explains that a 100-year flood is a flood level with a 1% or greater chance of being equaled or exceeded in any year, not one that happens once a century.

  • You can request flood information from the county floodplain administrator by giving the Randall appraisal ID, the address and the legal description.
  • The Flood Insurance Rate Map shows special flood hazard areas, and a Letter of Map Amendment can remove a property that was mapped in by mistake.
  • Under the county's floodplain rules, improvements or repairs costing 50% or more of a building's market value count as substantial improvement or substantial damage.
  • Building without required county floodplain permits can bring fines up to $500 per day.

Lenders can require flood insurance independently of a map change, so a buyer's lender has the final say.

What if the Amarillo house is inherited, behind on payments or rented?

Texas gives owners a few timelines to work with, and Panhandle counties follow the same rules as the rest of the state.

  • Inherited: an heir not on the recorded deed must give the appraisal district an affidavit of ownership interest, the death certificate and a recent utility bill to claim the homestead exemption.
  • Behind on payments: lenders generally wait until a loan is more than 120 days late. A notice of sale must go out at least 21 days ahead of the first-Tuesday auction.
  • Tenants: written notice to vacate is at least three days unless the lease says otherwise. Eviction cases are filed in justice court, and a writ of possession is available six days after judgment.

Each of these paths can end in a sale, and the earlier you pick one, the more room you have.

More questions about Amarillo, TX

Is Amarillo in Potter County or Randall County?

Both. The Handbook of Texas says the city is in southern Potter County and extends into Randall County, so a house's county depends on its parcel.

What is the due date for Randall County property tax?

On receipt. Pay by January 31 to avoid penalty and interest. Statements are mailed each October 1, and unpaid taxes are delinquent on February 1.

How much is a tax certificate in Randall County?

The fee is $10, paid with certified funds when you pick it up at the Canyon or Amarillo office. The certificate lists delinquent taxes for each taxing unit.

Does Amarillo require a Certificate of Occupancy?

Yes, under city ordinance Sec. 4-10-21. It is issued automatically for new buildings, and an existing property may need one if none was issued or the use changes.

What does a typical Amarillo owner-occupied home cost?

The Census Bureau's 2020-2024 median value for owner-occupied homes in Amarillo is $196,900.

Selling a house in Allen FAQ

How much is a house worth in Allen?

The Census Bureau's 2019-2023 survey puts the median value of owner-occupied homes in Allen at $429,900.

Which sale route suits an Allen homeowner?

An Allen owner has three routes: a brokered listing, a private sale, or a cash purchase. Which one fits depends on how much time and repair work the house can take. Allen lies in southwestern Collin County along U.S. Highway 75, and Census figures put it at 113,447 people in mid-2025.

Owners occupy roughly seven in ten Allen homes, so a well kept house meets many buyers who plan to live in it. A home with deferred repairs, a tenant, or a probate delay tends to suit a buyer comfortable with the condition and closes when the seller is ready.

  • Brokered listing: the widest exposure, with showings, lender-backed offers and inspection negotiations.
  • Private sale: you set the price and run the showings, and you also draft the paperwork.
  • Cash purchase: one buyer, a sale in present condition, and a closing date that you choose.

How expensive and how crowded is housing in Allen?

Allen is a high-income, high-value suburb with a large owner-occupied base. The city's QuickFacts table lists the figures below, and they frame what a typical buyer or renter in Allen looks like.

Allen city, Texas: selected Census Bureau QuickFacts figures
MeasureFigure
Resident estimate for mid-2025113,447
Census count, April 1, 2020104,627
Share of occupied homes held by their owners69.4%
Typical home value for owners (median), 2020-2024$464,100
Typical monthly rent (median gross)$1,932
Households, 2020-202437,243
Middle household income, 2020-2024$130,901
Average commute to work, 2020-202428.0 minutes
Land area, 202026.40 square miles

Table data come from the Census Bureau's Allen page on QuickFacts.

The city's population count was 84,246 in 2010, so Allen added roughly 20,000 residents in the decade that followed. The 2020 density was about 3,963 people per square mile, a compact suburban pattern.

How did Allen grow into the city it is today?

Allen began as a railroad stop. According to the Texas State Historical Association, an agent for the Houston and Texas Central Railway established the town in 1870, and it was named in 1872 for a former Texas attorney general who promoted the line. A post office opened in 1876, and by 1884 the settlement had a school, three churches, a chair factory and a flour mill.

Growth came late. The town had 1,940 residents in 1970 and 8,314 in 1980, a jump the Handbook of Texas ties to the economic growth of Dallas and Plano and the construction of Dallas-Fort Worth International Airport. By 2000 the population had reached 43,554.

That history explains the housing stock. Allen is a commuter city built mostly in the decades after 1970, so most sellers are dealing with homes that are decades old rather than a century old, and the questions that come up at sale are usually roofs, foundations and updates, not historic districts.

Which Allen city rules should a seller or landlord know about?

Allen has recently added a rental program that matters to anyone selling a house that was leased. At its October 13 meeting, the Allen City Council approved an ordinance creating a registration and inspection program for single-family rental properties, covering houses, townhomes and duplexes.

  • Annual registration fee: $150, with a $50 late registration fee.
  • Reinspection fee for ongoing compliance issues: $25.
  • The city planned to begin notifying owners in November 2026, and the initial registration deadline is January 31, 2027.
  • The city says single-family rentals make up about 14% of its housing but produced 38% of property violations, which is why exterior inspections are part of the program.

The city is matching ownership and utility billing records to find rentals. If you receive a notice for a house that is not a rental, the notice explains how to contact the city. If the home has been a short-term rental, ask Allen's permitting staff whether a rental permit is on file before you list.

For remodeling and repair permits, Allen's Building and Permitting Division is the first call. Open permits left behind by a prior owner can slow a closing, so ask for the permit history on the address.

Who bills the tax on an Allen house, and what changes at sale?

Collin County's tax assessor-collector sends the bill, and the Collin Central Appraisal District sets the value. Statements are mailed in October, and the county's page advises payment by January 31 to avoid penalties. The Property Tax Office is at 2300 Bloomdale Road, Suite 2324, McKinney, and the county says tax certificates and similar special requests are handled only at the McKinney location.

Exemption paperwork goes to the appraisal district. Its FAQ says the standard homestead form is accepted January 1 through April 30, never before, never by email, and never for a fee. Missing the window is not fatal: the district allows a late filing up to two years after the bill went delinquent.

The district's 2023 table of rates and exemptions listed these entries for Allen city, and the current year's table may differ:

  • Homestead: 5.00% of value, with a $5,000 floor.
  • Age 65 or older: $50,000.
  • Disabled person: $25,000.

Older sellers (65 and up) holding a school tax ceiling can carry the ceiling to a replacement Texas home as a percentage, according to Collin CAD. A buyer who moves in files a fresh homestead application of their own.

How is the deed recorded in Collin County?

The Collin County Clerk files Allen deeds. The clerk's land recordings page says to bring an original or a clerk-certified copy that is signed and notarized. It adds that House Bill 4350 led to redactions in parts of the online database, which is not the official repository of real property records.

Under Texas law, a deed has to be acknowledged before a notary or similar officer, or witnessed, before the clerk will record it. Fees vary by document and change over time, so request the current schedule from the clerk.

In most sales the title company orders the tax certificate, pays off mortgages and files the deed. Because a tax lien attaches each January 1, any earlier unpaid year must be cleared for the transfer to be clean.

What if the Allen house is inherited, in foreclosure or rented?

Three situations come up often, and each has a short set of Texas rules.

  • After a death: the court window for offering a will is four years. If nothing needs administering, a muniment of title lets heirs convey after the order and will are recorded with the clerk in the land's home county.
  • Behind on the mortgage: default notices give 20 days to reinstate, and a posted sale notice precedes the auction by 21 days or more.
  • Renters in the house: three days' written notice to vacate is the baseline unless the lease differs, followed by a justice court filing.

Closing before the auction date or before an eviction is finished leaves you more choices than waiting does.

What should I check before accepting an offer on an Allen home?

Put the following in writing before you sign.

  • A tax certificate from the Collin County office showing no earlier balance.
  • Confirmation from Collin CAD that your homestead and any ceiling are on file.
  • If tenants lived there, a check on the city's rental registration for the address.
  • A title search for open permits and unreleased liens.
  • The closing date and the fee split spelled out in the contract.

More questions about Allen, TX

Does Allen require rental houses to be registered?

Yes. The Allen City Council approved a registration and inspection program for single-family rentals, including houses, townhomes and duplexes. Annual registration costs $150, with a $50 late fee, and the first deadline is January 31, 2027.

Who collects property tax on an Allen home?

The Collin County Tax Assessor-Collector collects it. The Property Tax Office is in McKinney, and Collin Central Appraisal District sets the value and handles exemptions.

When can I apply for a homestead exemption on an Allen house?

File between January 1 and April 30 with Collin CAD. The district does not accept early or emailed applications and charges no fee, and a late application is allowed up to two years after the taxes become delinquent.

Can I sell an Allen house if property taxes are unpaid?

Yes, but the taxes have to be paid at or before closing. A tax lien attaches on January 1 each year, so the buyer cannot take clear title until the balance is cleared.

What is the Census population figure for Allen?

The bureau's mid-2025 estimate is 113,447 residents, up from 104,627 in the 2020 census.

Selling a house in Baytown FAQ

How much is a house worth in Baytown?

The Census Bureau's 2019-2023 survey puts the median value of owner-occupied homes in Baytown at $187,900.

Which selling routes make sense for a Baytown homeowner in a hurry?

A Baytown owner can hire an agent, go it alone, or hand the house to a cash buyer who accepts whatever condition it is in. Cash deals draw owners with a repair backlog, a property that came through an estate, a tenant situation they want to end, or a lender or court deadline.

Baytown had about 86,561 residents in mid-2025, and the 2020-2024 estimates say owners occupy 52.3 percent of homes. With a middle home value of $197,300, a long repair list can eat a big slice of what a listing would bring.

  • Hiring an agent: best for a sound house when you have time for open houses and loan approval.
  • Doing it yourself: you handle price, contract and buyer questions yourself, then close at a title company.
  • Cash buyer: no lender, no repair demands, and a closing date set after a short walk-through.

What turned a ferry crossing and an oil field into Baytown?

Baytown owes its shape to the refinery. The Handbook of Texas calls it a highly industrialized city of oil refining, rubber, chemical and carbon black plants, thirty miles east of downtown Houston on Interstate 10 and State Highway 146.

The area was isolated farmland until a 1908 oil strike beside Tabbs Bay. The nearby Goose Creek field became, in 1916, the first offshore drilling in Texas, and in 1917 the founders of Humble Oil and Refining bought about 2,200 acres for a refinery, with construction starting in 1919. The company laid out streets, supplied utilities, sold lots and financed employee homes, and the camp of tents and shacks became permanent in 1923. Pelly, Goose Creek and the Baytown site then merged, and the city was established on January 24, 1948.

Residents numbered 20,958 in 1948 and 67,117 in 1990, as the city stretched from 7.5 to more than 32 square miles. By the 2020 Census the land area was 37.00 square miles. A tunnel under the Houston Ship Channel opened in 1953 and gave way to the Fred Hartman Bridge in the mid-1990s. The Handbook lists Lee College and more than ten major petrochemical plants among the local institutions. Because the company financed employee homes in the 1920s, parts of the city started as company-supported housing, and buyers of older homes will ask about age, plumbing and foundation.

The older layers run deep. A ferry crossing at the junction of the San Jacinto River and Buffalo Bayou, set up in 1822, still operates, and a grant of more than 9,000 acres in 1824 covered most of present Baytown. The boundaries now run from near the San Jacinto River east into Chambers County and include former communities such as Cedar Bayou and Wooster.

What do income, rent and household figures say about Baytown?

The middle rent in Baytown is $1,307, while owners carry $1,761 a month with a loan or $691 once it is paid off. The typical household earned $59,910 in 2024 dollars, and the poverty rate was 18.2 percent.

Growth since 2020 has been slow, 1.2 percent over the 85,547 baseline, after the city rose from 71,802 residents in 2010. Of adults over 24, 78.6 percent finished high school and 14.8 percent hold a four-year degree.

Which county handles my Baytown property, Harris or Chambers?

It depends on the parcel. Baytown sits in southeastern Harris County and reaches east into Chambers County, so two sets of county offices serve the city.

The split decides who files your deed, who values the lot and who sends the bill. Look in the wrong county and your parcel simply will not show.

  • Read the top of your tax bill for the county and the account number.
  • Ask the closing agent which clerk will file the deed.
  • If you live near the county line, check which school and other districts show on the bill.

The Comptroller's property tax basics page says appraisal districts value property as of January 1 and bills go out around October 1.

Are nightly rentals allowed in Baytown, and does that affect a buyer?

Baytown's land development code has allowed nightly rentals in residential and mixed-use districts only with a Special Use Permit voted by City Council. The first request reached Council on December 11, 2025, and was approved with conditions for an existing house in a Suburban Residential district.

Staff then drafted a text amendment that would replace the permit vote with a standard permit process in those districts. A Planning and Zoning hearing was set for March 17, 2026, and a City Council hearing for April 23, 2026. Council also looked at annual permits and inspections and at limits on occupancy and parking.

If your house has hosted paying guests, ask Baytown planning staff which rule covers the address and whether any approval exists. A buyer counting on rental income should verify the status with the city before signing. The city's amendment notice describes the proposal.

What are the steps for selling a house left to me in Baytown?

Work out how title reaches you, since that decides what the insurer will accept. A will can be probated within four years of death, and a court may take a later filing for good reason.

  • Muniment of title: for an estate whose only debts are real-estate liens; the court order and will go to the clerk where the land sits.
  • Small estate affidavit: limited to $75,000 in assets outside the homestead, and generally no real property apart from a homestead passing to a spouse or minor children.
  • Affidavit of heirship: a sworn statement that no law forces a title company to take.
  • Executor's or administrator's deed: follows a court appointment.

Heirs missing from the recorded deed give the appraisal district an affidavit of ownership interest, a death certificate and a recent utility bill to keep a homestead exemption. The State Law Library's informal probate guide explains each path, and a probate lawyer can say which fits.

What happens to back taxes when a Baytown house sells?

Each year's tax lien attaches on January 1 and rides with the house, so any unpaid amount is taken from your sale money when you close. Bills are mailed in October, and accounts open on February 1 turn delinquent with a six percent penalty and one percent interest.

A homestead owner who has fallen behind can ask the collector about a payment plan, and some collectors offer up to 36 months. Penalty and interest may be waived in narrow cases if the tax is paid within 21 days of learning of the delinquency and a written request is made inside 181 days. Request a payoff number before choosing a closing date, and have the title company check for judgment liens.

More questions about Baytown, TX

Is Baytown in Harris or Chambers County?

Both. The city lies in southeastern Harris County and extends east into western Chambers County. Your tax bill names the county, which fixes where the deed is filed and which appraisal district values the lot.

Can I tell a buyer my Baytown house works as a nightly rental?

Only after checking with the city. Baytown has required a Special Use Permit approved by City Council, and a 2026 amendment proposed a permit process instead. Planning staff can say which rule applies to your address.

Is there a time limit to probate a will before I sell?

A will generally must be filed within four years of death, although a court can accept a later filing for good cause. A muniment of title order and the will then go to the clerk of the county where the property sits.

What is a typical home worth in Baytown?

About $197,300 for owner-occupied homes, according to the 2020-2024 Census estimates. That is a middle figure, so a particular house can land well above or below it with its size, age and repair needs.

What is Baytown's current population?

About 86,561 residents in July 2025, a 1.2 percent gain on the 2020 baseline. The city covers 37.00 square miles and counted 30,964 households in 2020-2024.

Selling a house in Anna FAQ

How much is a house worth in Anna?

The Census Bureau's 2019-2023 survey puts the median value of owner-occupied homes in Anna at $312,700.

Which selling routes make sense for an Anna homeowner?

Anna homeowners can sell through an agent, sell the house themselves, or take a direct cash offer, and the tradeoff is price against speed. Anna is in north central Collin County, and its population roughly doubled in five years, so many sellers are first owners of newer homes in subdivisions that still have active builders nearby.

That second fact shapes the sale. A buyer comparing your resale with a builder's model home on the same street will look closely at price, condition and any recurring assessment on the tax bill. A cash buyer skips that comparison and prices the home in its present condition.

  • An agent listing suits a clean, newer home when you can wait for a financed buyer.
  • A sale without an agent works if you are comfortable handling the contract and title paperwork.
  • A cash offer fits a quick move, an inherited house, a tenant situation or repairs you do not want to finance.

How fast is Anna growing, according to the Census Bureau?

Anna is one of the fastest-growing places in the county. The 2010 census counted 8,249 people in 2010 and 16,896 in 2020, then estimated 35,245 by mid-2025. Measured from its 2020 starting estimate, that is a gain of 105.7%.

Anna city, Texas: what the Census Bureau reports about its people and homes

Numbers above are from the Census Bureau's QuickFacts entry for Anna.

Anna's land area is 16.45 square miles. With a young age profile, larger households and a commute above half an hour, the typical Anna buyer is a family looking for space within reach of McKinney and the Dallas job market.

Where did Anna come from?

Anna is on State Highway 5 and Farm Road 455, about eleven miles northeast of McKinney, and it began with the railroad. The Texas State Historical Association says the Houston and Texas Central Railway passed through in 1873, and the town was platted in 1883 with twenty residents, two stores, a steam gristmill and a Baptist church.

Anna incorporated in 1913. For most of the twentieth century it stayed small: the Handbook of Texas gives 538 residents in 1929, 855 in the mid-1980s and 904 in 1990. The accounts of how it got its name differ, with several stories tied to the railroad's officials and a local founder's family.

Anna's growth is so recent that many of its houses are young as well. Questions that come up in these sales include expired builder warranties, drainage on newly graded lots and neighborhood-level assessments.

Do special districts or assessments affect an Anna sale?

They can. Anna's City Council creates public improvement districts by resolution, and the city's public documents include Resolution 2023-02-1378, approved February 14, 2023, creating The Woods at Lindsey Place Public Improvement District. A PID lets a city finance streets, utilities and similar improvements through assessments on the lots that benefit.

Collin County also has many municipal utility districts and water districts, and Collin CAD's rate table lists them as separate taxing entities. A house in one of these districts has an extra line on the property tax bill.

  • Have the title company check whether the lot is inside a PID or a utility district.
  • Ask the Collin County Tax Assessor-Collector which entities appear on your tax statement.
  • Ask the city for the PID's assessment schedule if the lot is inside one.
  • Give the buyer those figures early so the price conversation uses the real annual cost.

What permits and inspections does Anna require?

Anna's Building Department handles permits and inspections from the Municipal Complex at 120 W. 7th Street, Suite 142, open on weekdays from eight to five The city's permit information page lists requirements for fences, irrigation, remodels, roofing, solar panels, pools and spas, water heaters and patio covers.

Inspections are requested by email by 4 p.m. on the business day before, and none are done on weekends or holidays. The city also lists extra forms that may be required, including a site drainage acknowledgement, a homeowner's affidavit and a pool affidavit.

Before listing, the useful step is to confirm that any fence, pool, roof or remodel work done during your ownership was permitted and finaled. A buyer's inspector often asks, and a missing final can stall the closing. The Building Department phone is 972-924-2616.

How are Anna property taxes billed and when are they due?

Anna's property tax bill comes from the Collin County Tax Assessor-Collector. Statements go out in October and are treated as due when received, and the county says January 31 is the date to beat for avoiding penalties. Since a lien for the year attaches on January 1, the title company will ask that any balance be paid out of your proceeds.

In the 2023 table that Collin CAD published, Anna city offered the exemptions below. The district posts a new table each year, so confirm the current entries:

  • Homestead: 3.00% of value, with a $5,000 floor.
  • Age 65 or older: $30,000.
  • Disabled person: $30,000.

If you move in partway through a year, you may be able to claim the homestead exemption for the rest of that year when the prior owner held none. Owners with an age-based or disability exemption on school taxes have a ceiling on that bill, and Collin CAD says the ceiling can follow the owner to another Texas home as a percentage.

Homestead appraisals are capped at 10% growth a year, plus new improvements. The cap limits taxable value, so a long-time owner's bill can trail the market price of the house.

What changes when an Anna house is inherited or facing foreclosure?

Collin County offices handle the filings, and the state rules are short.

  • Heirs: someone who inherited but is not on the recorded deed can still claim the homestead exemption by giving the appraisal district a sworn statement of ownership, the death certificate and a recent utility bill. The small-estate route is closed when the estate holds real property other than a homestead.
  • Lender action: a sale notice must precede the first-Tuesday auction by 21 days or more, and a borrower can cure within 20 days of the default letter.
  • Deeds: the Collin County Clerk accepts originals or certified copies that are signed and notarized.

Where time is short, a sale before the auction date lets you set the closing timeline yourself. A cash buyer has no loan approval to wait for, which can shorten the calendar.

More questions about Anna, TX

How big is Anna, Texas?

The Census Bureau estimated 35,245 residents on July 1, 2025, more than double the 2020 estimates base of 17,137, and the city has 16.45 square miles of land.

Is a PID assessment passed to the buyer when I sell an Anna house?

Yes, an assessment attached to the lot stays with the property. Ask the title company and the city for the schedule, and share it with buyers up front.

Which county office collects tax for Anna?

The Collin County Tax Assessor-Collector bills and collects it. Collin Central Appraisal District, in McKinney, sets the value and processes exemptions.

Should I gather permit records before listing in Anna?

It is not a statutory step, but buyers and inspectors ask for it. Anna's Building Department can tell you which permits were issued and whether they were finaled.

Can an heir claim the homestead exemption on an inherited Anna house?

Yes. Heirs not named on a recorded deed file an affidavit of ownership interest with the appraisal district, along with the death certificate and a recent utility bill.

Selling a house in Alvin FAQ

How much is a house worth in Alvin?

The Census Bureau's 2019-2023 survey puts the median value of owner-occupied homes in Alvin at $212,500.

What speeds up a home sale in Alvin?

Selling quickly in Alvin comes down to three things: a clear tax and title picture, honest disclosure of storm and flood history, and a buyer who can close on your timeline. Alvin is in northeast Brazoria County, about twelve miles southeast of Houston, and its sellers work with Brazoria County offices for taxes and deeds.

Alvin has grown from 21,413 residents in 2000 to a 2025 estimate of 30,115. Owners usually choose between an agent listing, a direct sale, and a cash offer. A cash offer is the shortest path when a house needs repairs, has been through water damage, is inherited, or carries a tenant, because the buyer takes the property as it stands.

  • Agent listing: best for a move-in ready house when you can wait for a financed buyer.
  • Direct sale: you handle the buyer, the contract and the title steps.
  • Cash offer: one buyer, no lender, and a closing date set around your plans.

How does Alvin compare on the Census numbers?

Alvin is a mid-sized, more affordable suburb south of Houston. QuickFacts paints the following picture, with 30,115 residents estimated for 2025, an 11.7% rise over the 2020 base.

Alvin city, Texas: Census Bureau housing and income figures
MeasureFigure
Owner share of occupied housing60.9%
Typical home value for owners (median), 2020-2024$228,700
Typical monthly cost for owners with a mortgage$2,029
Typical monthly rent (median gross)$1,215
Households, 2020-202410,456
Middle household income, 2020-2024$71,477
Persons without health insurance, under 6518%
Average commute to work, 2020-202429.4 minutes

Figures come from the QuickFacts page the Census Bureau keeps for Alvin.

About four in ten Alvin homes are rented, which means a house can sell to an investor as easily as to a family. Alvin's land area is 24.30 square miles, and the 2020 census tallied 27,098 people.

Why does Alvin's storm history matter to a seller?

Alvin began as a Santa Fe Railroad flag station in the 1860s near the head of Mustang Slough, on the Galveston-to-Richmond branch. The Texas State Historical Association says Santa Fe hired Alvin Morgan in 1872 to supervise cattle loading at the stock pens, and the settlement took his first name after a postal naming conflict. Alvin was incorporated in 1891 and again in 1893.

Farming and fruit growing carried the early economy, followed by livestock, dairying, rice, oil, natural gas and petrochemicals. The city became an independent school district in 1925 and grew 89 percent between 1960 and 1970, from 5,643 to 10,671 residents. By 2000 it had 21,413.

The same entry notes that each year from July through November Alvin braces for floods, hurricanes and tornadoes. The 1900 Galveston hurricane destroyed or damaged most of the city's businesses and homes, tropical storm Claudette dropped forty-three inches of rain near Alvin in twenty-four hours in 1979, and Alicia battered the area four years later. For a seller, that record is the reason buyers ask about flood history and insurance.

What storm and flood questions will buyers ask in Alvin?

Expect questions about elevation, past water in the house, roof age and wind rating. The City of Alvin's permit page says its adopted codes use a wind load of 140 mph from the code table, and that new construction needs engineer-sealed drawings, a survey and a plot plan.

  • Ask the City of Alvin's engineering and permit staff which flood zone the lot is in, and keep any elevation certificate you have.
  • Keep records of past repairs, including who did the work and whether a permit was pulled.
  • Find out whether the house is covered by flood insurance and what the premium has been.
  • If you rebuilt after storm damage, keep the final inspection record.

Brazoria County also gives owners in a declared disaster area a payment option on their tax bill, described below, which can matter if the house was damaged in a storm that year.

What do Alvin's permit rules mean when I sell?

The City of Alvin requires permits and inspections for new construction, remodeling and repairs. A homeowner who wants to remodel or repair has to show proof of a homestead exemption before buying a permit, so a house that was permitted by a prior owner should have that history on file.

Inspection requests need 24 hours' notice, and permits and inspections go through the city's online MyGov portal. Driveways and driveway culverts need a permit, residential driveways can be 12 to 24 feet wide, and enclosing the front ditch is not allowed. If the property fronts a state highway, TxDOT also has to issue a permit.

If you replaced a driveway, added a room or finished a garage while you owned the house, ask the city's permit office whether the permit was closed. Unclosed permits are one of the common reasons a closing slips.

How do Brazoria County property taxes work for an Alvin seller?

The Brazoria County Tax Assessor-Collector sends tax bills, while the Brazoria Central Appraisal District in Angleton (500 N Chenango Street) values property and processes exemptions. The district keeps weekday hours from eight until four-thirty, and its main line is 979-849-7792.

The county tax office lets owners spread payment in several ways:

  • Half pay: half by November 30, the rest by June 30 of the next year.
  • Age and disability plan: four equal installments, due January 31, March 31, May 31 and July 31, for qualifying homesteads and unmarried surviving spouses.
  • Disaster plan: the same four installments for owners whose property was damaged in a declared disaster area.
  • Deferral: homeowners 65 or over, or disabled, can postpone payment by signing an affidavit at the appraisal district; 5 percent interest accrues each year.
  • Partial payments: any amount is accepted, and only the unpaid remainder draws penalty and interest.

A deferral comes due once the owner stops owning and living in the home, so a sale triggers it. Tell the title company about any deferral or installment plan early so the payoff figure is right.

A buyer who moves in applies at the appraisal district with a driver's license or state ID showing the property address. A seller with a school tax ceiling can ask the district they are leaving for a certificate to carry the ceiling to a new county.

How does a probate or foreclosure sale work in Alvin?

Filings for an Alvin property go through Brazoria County.

  • Estates: a will should be offered for probate within four years of death. If no administration is needed, heirs can use a muniment of title, filing the court order and will with the county clerk.
  • Mortgage default: on most home loans the lender must wait until the loan is more than 120 days behind, then allow 20 days to cure, then give at least 21 days' notice of the sale.
  • Tax sales: a former owner of a homestead sold at a tax sale has two years from the filing of the purchaser's deed to redeem, per a Texas Supreme Court opinion.

Selling ahead of an auction date keeps the choice of buyer in your hands.

More questions about Alvin, TX

Is Alvin, Texas in a flood-prone area?

Parts of it are, and the city's history includes major storms. The Handbook of Texas says residents face floods, hurricanes and tornadoes from July through November. Ask the City of Alvin which flood zone your lot is in.

Can I pay my Alvin property taxes in installments?

Yes, in some cases. Brazoria County offers a split payment, a four-installment plan for over-65, disabled and disabled veteran homesteads, a four-installment plan for disaster-area owners, deferral for older or disabled owners and partial payments.

Is a permit required for work on my Alvin house?

Yes for new construction, remodeling and repairs, and also for driveways and culverts. Homeowners must show proof of a homestead exemption before buying a permit.

Who sets the value of my Alvin home for tax purposes?

The Brazoria Central Appraisal District. Its office is on N Chenango Street in Angleton, and owners apply there for homestead and age-based exemptions.

What population does the Census Bureau estimate for Alvin?

The Census Bureau estimated 30,115 residents on July 1, 2025.

Many sales here involve family homes held for decades, houses that came through an estate, or rentals that a landlord is tired of managing.

  • Market listing: works if the house shows well and a lender signs off on the buyer.
  • Investor purchase: skips showings and loan approval, and usually the repair list too.
  • Payoffs first: a mortgage, tax balance or code fine is paid from the proceeds, so get each figure in writing before you accept anything.

Where did Balch Springs come from, and why are its houses mostly postwar?

Balch Springs began as a cluster of farms around a spring and became a commuter suburb of Dallas, which is why most of its houses date from the postwar decades. The Texas State Historical Association says the community was founded around 1870 when the family of John Balch settled by three springs, one of which never ran dry.

Residents incorporated the town on June 13, 1953, with a mayor-council government, in order to avoid annexation by Dallas. The population was about 3,500 in 1956, 13,050 by 1976, 17,406 in 1990 and 19,375 in 2000. Interstate 635 made the drive to Dallas faster in the 1970s, and by the late 1970s about 95 percent of working residents commuted to Dallas or Garland.

The town sits on Interstates 635 and 20 and U.S. Highway 175, ten miles southeast of Dallas in Dallas County. Hickory Creek rises here. By 1991 the town had seventeen manufacturers, including makers of shipping pallets and machine parts. In 1988 residents voted to combine with Mesquite, but the vote was ruled invalid and Balch Springs remained independent. In earlier decades children attended school in either the Dallas or Mesquite districts, so ask the county appraisal district which school district taxes your parcel.

How do Balch Springs household and housing figures compare with other places?

A typical owned home in Balch Springs was valued at $224,400 in the 2020-2024 estimates, and a typical renter paid $1,378 a month. The city's population estimate for mid-2025 is 27,258, which is 1.6 percent under the 27,705 baseline for April 2020 but well above the 23,728 counted in 2010.

Nine square miles hold 3,067.9 people per square mile. About 91.9 percent of residents kept the same address through the prior year, and the 33.7 minute commute is a reminder that many workers travel some distance for their jobs.

Does Balch Springs require rental registration or a certificate of occupancy?

Yes. The city's permit requirements sheet lists both a rental registration and a certificate of occupancy, and a seller with a tenant or an investor buyer should expect to deal with each.

  • Rental registration: the applicant needs a driver's license and proof of ownership, such as closing paperwork or a deed in the applicant's name. The registration must be renewed every two years.
  • Inspection timing: the city says rental inspections must be done before a tenant moves in, or the owner incurs a violation fee.
  • Certificate of occupancy: the applicant provides a driver's license, a lease or proof of ownership, a site map and a floor plan.

Because registration is tied to the owner's name and deed, an investor who keeps the tenant files a new registration once the deed is recorded. Contact the Permits and Inspections Division at 972-286-4477 to ask what is on file for your address. Inspection requests are sent by email to inspections@balchspringstx.gov, per the city's permits page.

What city permits and sign-offs come up when a Balch Springs house changes hands?

The city's permit sheet shows what a seller or investor buyer may need: a certificate of occupancy takes a lease or proof of ownership, a site map and a floor plan, while electrical, plumbing and air conditioning work each need their own permit pulled by a registered master contractor. Roof work can be a same-day permit when no structural work is involved, and the sheet lists the current codes as the 2021 IRC and IBC and the 2020 NEC.

For an estate or moving sale, note the garage sale rules on the same sheet: three sales a calendar year, with 90 days between them. Contractors working on the house must be registered with the city, so check that anyone you hire for pre-sale repairs is on the list. Reach Permits and Inspections at 972-286-4477, and send inspection requests to the email address on the city's permits page.

Can an open city notice get in the way of selling in Balch Springs?

An open notice is not a bar to selling, but it stays with the property and ought to be cleared or discussed before closing. Officers walk the neighborhoods every day and also act on complaints.

The first letter allows 10 days to fix the problem, shortened to 7 days for tall grass and solid waste, and it remains active for 12 months. If a return visit finds no change, the officer writes a Notice to Appear that lists the ordinance, the fine and how to reach the court. Owners can ask the department for more time to complete a repair.

Before you list, walk the lot with the city's Top 10 violations list, which the Code Enforcement page offers in English and Spanish. Disclose any citation or court date to a buyer, so the closing is not held up.

How much time do I have to sell before a foreclosure auction?

Most Texas home loans can be foreclosed without a lawsuit, and the calendar is strict enough that a sale before the auction is often workable. Federal servicing rules generally hold off a first filing until the loan is over 120 days delinquent.

  • A borrower can reinstate by paying what is past due within 20 days after the default notice arrives.
  • The servicer then sends a sale notice at least 21 days ahead, posts it at the courthouse and files it with the county clerk.
  • Auctions run on a month's first Tuesday, with a window from 10 a.m. until 4 p.m.
  • A lender can sue for a shortfall within two years, and the borrower can ask for a credit for the home's fair market value.

The Dallas County commissioners court sets where auctions are held, so ask the county clerk for the spot. A sale that closes before the first Tuesday can pay off the loan from the proceeds. The State Law Library's foreclosure guide walks through each stage.

How does a tenant change the sale of a Balch Springs house?

Give each buyer a copy of the lease, since its terms govern what a new owner can do about the occupant. If you need the tenant gone before closing, a written notice to vacate normally allows at least three days unless the lease sets another period.

An eviction suit goes to justice court. The tenant must be served four days or more before trial, and a hearing is set 10 to 21 days after filing. A losing party can appeal to county court within five days, and a writ of possession waits at least six days after final judgment. Many owners with tenants simply pick a buyer who will keep the tenant, which skips that timeline.

More questions about Balch Springs, TX

Must I keep my rental registered until the Balch Springs sale closes?

Yes, while the house is rented. The registration lasts two years and requires an inspection before a tenant moves in. A buyer who keeps renting registers in their own name with proof of ownership.

How soon must a Balch Springs code notice be fixed?

Ten days for most notices and seven days for tall grass or solid waste. If a return inspection still finds the problem, a citation with a fine and court date follows. A written extension request is allowed.

Where is the deed filed for a Balch Springs sale?

With the Dallas County clerk, since the city lies in Dallas County. The deed must be signed and acknowledged before a notary or other authorized officer.

Is it too late to sell once the lender posts a foreclosure notice?

Not if the sale closes first. The borrower has 20 days from the default notice to reinstate, and the lender owes at least 21 days' notice of sale. Count back from the first Tuesday of the month.

How many people call Balch Springs home?

An estimated 27,258 people as of July 2025, in 8,247 households counted in 2020-2024. That is 1.6 percent below the April 2020 baseline, across 9.02 square miles.
